questions.question: How do you test React components — what do you test and with what tools?
questions.title: Testing React Basics
questions.direct_answer: Test BEHAVIOR, not implementation: render the component, interact with it as a user would (click, type), assert on what the user perceives (visible text, roles, states). React Testing Library is the standard: render() mounts into jsdom, queries by role/text/label (getByRole, getByText — accessible queries), userEvent simulates real interactions, and screen/assertions verify output. Jest or Vitest run the tests. Structure: Arrange (render) → Act (userEvent) → Assert (expect on rendered output).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Arrange: render + mock boundary] --> B[Act: userEvent — type, click]
    B --> C[Assert: screen — by role / text / label]
    B -.async.-> F[findBy* — waits for appearance]
    subgraph philosophy
        P[query like a user: roles + labels] --> N[not markup, not state, not classes]
    end
    U[unit: pure logic — table-driven] --> I[integration: component + mocked server] --> E[E2E: real browser, critical journeys]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why RTL won over Enzyme (the history worth knowing): Enzyme tested internals — shallow-render components, read their state, invoke their instance methods. It coupled tests to implementation, so refactoring a class component to hooks (or useState to useReducer) broke every test while changing NOTHING the user sees. RTL's founding principle: the closer your tests are to how the software is used, the more they can be trusted. Queries see only what the user sees. The ecosystem consolidated: RTL is the React-recommended standard, Enzyme died with React 17's incompatibilities.

The mocking boundary (the judgment layer): mock the NETWORK (msw — intercept fetch at the service-worker level, serve fixtures by route), not the FETCH CALL SITES (jest.mock of the api module couples tests to the import graph). MSW keeps components using their real fetch code and makes tests describe the server contract. Mock the outermost boundary — time (jest.useFakeTimers for debounce tests), randomness, and the specific third-party widget you can't run in jsdom — never your own internal seams.

The coverage honesty (the close): coverage measures what code RAN, not what was ASSERTED — delete every expect and coverage stays green. Use it to find untested error paths, not as a target. A pragmatic suite: a few component behavior tests per feature, table-driven unit tests for pure logic (reducers, formatters, validators — the highest ROI tests in any app), and one E2E (Playwright/Cypress) for each critical user journey — the 5% of tests that catch the integration bugs no lower layer sees.

I check the inputs and the expected result, trace the important state step by step, and add a test for the failure.
